Generalized discrete convolution, is defined as:

  • If d=1d = 1d=1﻿, this equation defines the discrete convolution over vectors
  • if d=2d = 2d=2﻿ it corresponds to the discrete convolution over matrices,
  • If d>2d > 2d>2﻿ it defines the discrete convolution over d-dimensional tensors.
  • The generalised discrete convolution satisfies the same properties of discrete convolutions, such as commutativity, linearity and translation invariance.

The generalized discrete cross-correlation

  • To convolve f with g, operationally we flip g on all its d axes. In correlation we don’t to this step

Cross Correlation is not commutative

If one function is symmetric f[u]=f[−u]f[u] = f[-u]f[u]=f[−u]﻿, cross-correlation and convolution are equal

Instead of shifting the window one entry at a time, we can do so with a larger step, also known as stride.

For example, suppose that the input image f[x,y]=Z100×100f [x, y] = Z^{100 \times 100}f[x,y]=Z100×100﻿ filter is 3×3

  • The size of the output image with a stride of 1 is 100−3+1=98100−3+1 = 98100−3+1=98﻿ (98×98 pixels)
  • The size of the output image with a stride of 2 is (100−3+1)/2=49(100 − 3 +1)/2 = 49(100−3+1)/2=49﻿

In convolutional neural networks the scaling of an image is implemented with a special non-trainable mechanism, referred to as pooling layer.

  • The role of a pooling layer is to reduce the dimension of an input figure f[c,x,y]f[c,x,y]f[c,x,y]﻿ in an output figure g[c,x′,y′]g[c,x′,y′]g[c,x′,y′]﻿ while maintaining the same number of channels
  • Fixed a channel, a pooling layer πππ﻿:

Types of Pooling:

  1. Max Pooling
  1. Avg Pooling
  1. First Pooling (not used in CNN but in IR) → first element of the patch

Why not everything is implemented with 2 FC hidden layers (as approx. theorem guarantees)?

  • Because the number of neurons grow exponentially with the number of input-output → impossible to train

How many kernels do we need? That is equivalent to say how many pattern are there?

  • The answer is provided by the manifold hypothesis: real-world data lives in a low-dimensional manifold (is valid for any type of representation, like text, images, video, music, …)
  • We exploit all the correlations and dependencies of the pixels
  • E.g. if we have 100x100 pixels we would never have all the possible compinations

AlexNet with 1k classes

A version of AlexNet with 16 convolutional layers is VGGNet19

Features produced by CNN convolutional layers can be flattened and used as image/patch descriptors.

  • Their semantic meaning depends on how the CNN was trained, typically for image classification
  • Unlike handcrafted descriptors such as SIFT, CNN features are not inherently invariant to rotation and scale.
    • Scale invariance is partially achieved through pooling operations, while rotation invariance usually requires data augmentation during training.
    • As a result, in content-based image retrieval (CBIR), there is still no clear consensus on whether CNN features consistently outperform SIFT descriptors.

One of the most well-known neural networks for object detection is YOLO (“You Only Look Once”). The image is divided into a regular S×SS \times SS×S﻿, each cell responsible for detecting an object whose center falls within it.

  • The YOLO architecture comprises convolutional and pooling layers followed by fully connected layers, and outputs a tensor of size S×S×(5B+C)S×S×(5B+C)S×S×(5B+C)﻿, where BBB﻿ is the number of bounding boxes per cell, each defined by four coordinates and a confidence score, and CCC﻿ is the number of object classes

Semantic segmentation → pixel classification

  1. For each pixel in the image, we extract a patch with a window centered on the pixel, and we use the patch to classify the pixel with a CNN model such as AlexNet.
  1. Design the CNN without downsampling → computationally expensive
  1. Introduce an up-sampling part:
    1. Simple unpooling replicates each input value across the corresponding output sub-region
    1. bed-of-nails unpooling places the value in a fixed position (typically the top-left) and sets all other elements to zero
    1. Max unpooling preserves spatial structure by reusing the locations of maxima from a previous max-pooling operation.
    1. transposed convolution performs learned upsampling using trainable kernels instead of fixed unpooling rules.
